questions.question_text: The line $L_{2}$ passing through $(3,-1)$ divides the line segment $L_{1}$ joining the points $(-1,2)$ and $(3,6)$ in the ratio $1:3$ internally. The equation of line $L_{2}$ is:
questions.question_html: The line $L_{2}$ passing through $(3,-1)$ divides the line segment $L_{1}$ joining the points $(-1,2)$ and $(3,6)$ in the ratio $1:3$ internally. The equation of line $L_{2}$ is:
questions.explanation_text: Let the points on line segment $L_{1}$ be $A(-1,2)\text{and}B(3,6)$ The line $L_{2}$ divides this segment internally in the ratio $1:3$ . Using the section formula, the point of division $P$ is $P(\frac{1 \cdot 3+3 \cdot (-1)}{1+3},\frac{1 \cdot 6+3 \cdot 2}{1+3})$ $P(\frac{3-3}{4},\frac{6+6}{4})$ $P(0,3)$ So, line $L_{2}$ passes through the points $(3,-1)$ and $(0,3)$ . Now find its slope: $m=\frac{3-(-1)}{0-3}$ $m=\frac{4}{-3}=-\frac{4}{3}$ Using point-slope form with point $(0,3)$ : $y-3=-\frac{4}{3}(x-0)$ $3y-9=-4x$ $4x+3y-9=0$ So, the equation of line $L_{2}$ is $4x+3y-9=0$ Correct option: Option C.
questions.explanation_html:
Let the points on line segment $L_{1}$ be

$A(-1,2)\text{and}B(3,6)$

The line $L_{2}$ divides this segment internally in the ratio $1:3$ .

Using the section formula, the point of division $P$ is

$P(\frac{1 \cdot 3+3 \cdot (-1)}{1+3},\frac{1 \cdot 6+3 \cdot 2}{1+3})$

$P(\frac{3-3}{4},\frac{6+6}{4})$

$P(0,3)$

So, line $L_{2}$ passes through the points $(3,-1)$ and $(0,3)$ .

Now find its slope:

$m=\frac{3-(-1)}{0-3}$

$m=\frac{4}{-3}=-\frac{4}{3}$

Using point-slope form with point $(0,3)$ :

$y-3=-\frac{4}{3}(x-0)$

$3y-9=-4x$

$4x+3y-9=0$

So, the equation of line $L_{2}$ is

$4x+3y-9=0$

Correct option: Option C.

Notice that the second equation is just twice the first:

First equation:

$4x+6y=5$

Multiply both sides by 2:

$8x+12y=10$

Since both equations represent the same line, there are infinitely many solutions.

Answer: Option B.

questions.question_html: The angle between the line $x+y=3$ and the line joining the points $(1,1)$ and $(-3,4)$ is

questions.question_html: If the straight line $2x-3y+17=0$ is perpendicular to the line passing through the points $(7,17)$ and $(15,\beta)$ , then $\beta$ equals
questions.explanation_text: Equation of line passing through $(7,17)$ and $(15,\beta)$ is $\begin{aligned} & (y-17)=(\frac{\beta-17}{15-7})(x-7) \\ \Rightarrow & y-17=\frac{(\beta-17)}{8}(x-7) \\ \Rightarrow & y=(\frac{\beta-17}{8})x-\frac{7(\beta-17)}{8}+17 \end{aligned}$ On comparing to $y=mx+c$ , we get Slope, $m_{1}=\frac{\beta-17}{8}$ It is given that above line is perpendicular to $2x-3y+17=0$ $\Rightarrow y=\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{17}{3}$ $\therefore$ Slope, $m_{2}=\frac{2}{3}$ Condition for perpendicular lines, $m_{1} \cdot m_{2}=-1$ $\begin{aligned} & (\frac{\beta-17}{8}) \times \frac{2}{3}=-1 \\ \Rightarrow & \beta-17=-12 \Rightarrow \beta=5 \end{aligned}$

Equation of line passing through $(7,17)$ and $(15,\beta)$ is

$\begin{aligned} & (y-17)=(\frac{\beta-17}{15-7})(x-7) \\ \Rightarrow & y-17=\frac{(\beta-17)}{8}(x-7) \\ \Rightarrow & y=(\frac{\beta-17}{8})x-\frac{7(\beta-17)}{8}+17 \end{aligned}$

On comparing to $y=mx+c$ , we get Slope, $m_{1}=\frac{\beta-17}{8}$

It is given that above line is perpendicular to

$2x-3y+17=0$

$\Rightarrow y=\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{17}{3}$

$\therefore$ Slope, $m_{2}=\frac{2}{3}$

Condition for perpendicular lines, $m_{1} \cdot m_{2}=-1$

$\begin{aligned} & (\frac{\beta-17}{8}) \times \frac{2}{3}=-1 \\ \Rightarrow & \beta-17=-12 \Rightarrow \beta=5 \end{aligned}$

Given,

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Point}(x_{1},y_{1})=(acos^{3}\theta,asin^{3}\theta) \\ & \text{Other line} \Rightarrow xsec\theta+ycosec\theta=a \\ & y=-\frac{xsec\theta}{cosec\theta}+\frac{a}{cosec\theta} \\ & \Rightarrow y=(-\frac{sin\theta}{cos\theta})x+asin\theta \\ & \Rightarrow y=m_{1}x+c \\ & \therefore m_{1}=-\frac{sin\theta}{cos\theta} \end{aligned}$

Equation of required line

$\Rightarrow (y-y_{1})=m(x-x_{1})$

$\text{where}m=\frac{cos\theta}{sin\theta}[ \because m_{1} \cdot m=-1,m=-\frac{1}{m_{1}}=-\frac{1}{(-\frac{sin\theta}{cos\theta})}=\frac{cos\theta}{sin\theta}]$

$\begin{aligned} & (y-asin^{3}\theta)=\frac{cos\theta}{sin\theta}(x-acos^{3}\theta) \\ & \Rightarrow ysin\theta-asin^{4}\theta=xcos\theta-acos^{4}\theta \\ & \Rightarrow xcos\theta-ysin\theta=a(cos^{4}\theta-sin^{4}\theta) \\ & =a(cos^{2}\theta+sin^{2}\theta)(cos^{2}\theta-sin^{2}\theta) \\ & =a \cdot (1) \cdot (cos2\theta)=acos2\theta \\ & \Rightarrow xcos\theta-ysin\theta=acos2\theta \end{aligned}$

questions.question_text: The equation of the line parallel to the line $3x-4y+2=0$ and passing through $(-2,3)$ is
questions.question_html: The equation of the line parallel to the line $3x-4y+2=0$ and passing through $(-2,3)$ is
questions.explanation_text: To find the equation of a line parallel to the given line $3x-4y+2=0$ that passes through the point $(-2,3)$ , follow these steps: Identify the form of the parallel line: A line parallel to $3x-4y+2=0$ will have the same coefficients for $x$ and $y$ . Thus, the equation of the line we are looking for can be written as: $3x-4y=\lambda$ Determine $\lambda$ using the given point: Since the line passes through the point $(-2,3)$ , substitute these coordinates into the equation: $3(-2)-4(3)=\lambda$ Calculate $\lambda$ : $-6-12=\lambda⟹\lambda=-18$ Write the equation of the line: Substitute $\lambda=-18$ back into the equation of the line: $3x-4y=-18$ Express the equation in standard form: Rewrite the equation as: $3x-4y+18=0$ Therefore, the equation of the line parallel to the given line and passing through the point $(-2,3)$ is $3x-4y+18=0$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To find the equation of a line parallel to the given line $3x-4y+2=0$ that passes through the point $(-2,3)$ , follow these steps:

Identify the form of the parallel line:

A line parallel to $3x-4y+2=0$ will have the same coefficients for $x$ and $y$ . Thus, the equation of the line we are looking for can be written as:

$3x-4y=\lambda$

Determine $\lambda$ using the given point:

Since the line passes through the point $(-2,3)$ , substitute these coordinates into the equation:

$3(-2)-4(3)=\lambda$

Calculate $\lambda$ :

$-6-12=\lambda⟹\lambda=-18$

Write the equation of the line:

Substitute $\lambda=-18$ back into the equation of the line:

$3x-4y=-18$

Express the equation in standard form:

Rewrite the equation as:

$3x-4y+18=0$

Therefore, the equation of the line parallel to the given line and passing through the point $(-2,3)$ is $3x-4y+18=0$ .

questions.question_text: Equation of line passing through the point $(1,2)$ and perpendicular to the line $y=3x-1$
questions.question_html: Equation of line passing through the point $(1,2)$ and perpendicular to the line $y=3x-1$
questions.explanation_text: Given the line equation: $y=3x-1$ The slope of this line is $3$ . To find the equation of a line perpendicular to this, we need the negative reciprocal of the given line's slope. Thus, the slope of the perpendicular line is: $-\frac{1}{3}$ The equation of a line with this slope that passes through the point $(1,2)$ can be set up using the point-slope form: $y-2=-\frac{1}{3}(x-1)$ Expanding this equation, we get: $3(y-2)=-(x-1)$ Which simplifies to: $3y-6=-x+1$ Rearranging terms, we arrive at: $x+3y-7=0$ This is the equation of the line that passes through the point $(1,2)$ and is perpendicular to $y=3x-1$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given the line equation:

$y=3x-1$

The slope of this line is $3$ .

To find the equation of a line perpendicular to this, we need the negative reciprocal of the given line's slope. Thus, the slope of the perpendicular line is:

$-\frac{1}{3}$

The equation of a line with this slope that passes through the point $(1,2)$ can be set up using the point-slope form:

$y-2=-\frac{1}{3}(x-1)$

Expanding this equation, we get:

$3(y-2)=-(x-1)$

Which simplifies to:

$3y-6=-x+1$

Rearranging terms, we arrive at:

$x+3y-7=0$

This is the equation of the line that passes through the point $(1,2)$ and is perpendicular to $y=3x-1$ .
